Spoilers for Focker In-Law are ahead! You can see the movie in theaters now.

Between Robert De Niro and Blythe Danner and Dustin Hoffman and Barbra Streisand, the Meet the Parents franchise has set a precedent for iconic parent casting. Now, following the release of Focker In-Law on the 2026 movie schedule, it seems like we could meet the parents of Ariana Grande’s Olivia at some point. So, with the final lines of the movie setting that up, I had to ask the cast and director about who could possibly play her mom and dad.

In Focker In-Law, after Olivia and Ben Stiller’s Greg clear the air and figure everything out, she notes that it’s time to meet her parents. And considering Focker In-Law is the fourth Focker film, I figured it’d only be natural if we got a Meet the Fockers-like sequel but with Olivia’s family.

So, when I interviewed the actors who play Ben Stiller’s kids (and son-in-law) in Focker In-Law, I had to ask who could play Grande’s parents. Beanie Feldstein, who plays Samantha, had a great idea for Olivia’s mom, saying:

I have one for her mom, which is Bernadette Peters. I really think that hits. That hits strong.

Now, moving on to her dad. Skyler Gisondo, who plays Henry (and Olivia’s fiancé by the end of the film), had a pretty wild idea for who could play that part, as he said:

What if Ben put on like this total prosthetic and did just old school play like seven characters.

I know he’s joking, but the idea of Ben Stiller doing what Mike Myers does in Austin Powers and playing a bunch of different characters would be hilarious.

Anyway, getting back to slightly more realistic answers, Eduardo Franco, who plays Samantha’s partner Eduardo in the movie, said Grande’s dad needs to be a “funny dude.” He also said:

I'm trying to think, man. It's gonna be funny. It's funny, dude. It's gotta be also probably into like singing and dancing and stuff. I'm trying to think.

Feldstein went on to note that “Olivia doesn’t sing or dance.” However, Franco lovingly said Grande does – as we all well know from her remarkable career as a pop star and her amazing work in the Wicked movies, which you can stream with a Disney+ subscription. So, whoever plays her dad has “got to be capable of what Ari can do.”

After that, the interview moved on, but toward the end of it, Franco finally came up with an idea for who could play Grande’s dad and blurted:

Javier Bardem. I'm sorry. I'm sorry. I'm sorry. I'm sorry. Sorry. This whole time I've been. I'm so sorry. I've been thinking. He's Spanish, Español, but I mean, he'd be just as intimidating.

You know what? I see the vision. Javier Bardem could totally go toe to toe with Robert De Niro’s Jack. Plus, the idea of Ben Stiller’s Greg trying to keep up with him is already making me laugh.

Now, when I asked John Hamburg, the writer and director of Focker In-Law, this question about Grande’s parents, he was far more tight-lipped. He wouldn’t give me any clues, but he did say there have been conversations about it:

OK, I love CinemaBlend, and there's no way I'm going to share that information with you. I do have some people swirling around, and we even talked on set, you know, with Ben and Ari and Bob about who could possibly play her parents. But listen, I'm just trying to get through the release of this movie, OK? So I can't share yet.

Considering the movie ends on a big tease about who Olivia’s parents could be, I certainly hope we get an answer someday. However, for now, I’m just happy they’re all thinking about it.

So, while we wait to see if we get to Meet the Joneses, I’ll be picturing Javier Bardem and Bernadette Peters as Ariana Grande’s parents and hoping that the cast’s ideas actually pan out.

#3728. Warhammer 40,000: Space Marine 2's latest updates introduces a Weekly Clash mode that shakes up PvP with some constricting modifiers

In as booming a monster truck rally commentator voice as you can imagine: ARE YOU READY TO GET DECIMATED??? Yes? Yippee! Because I've got some good news for you. The latest update for Warhammer 40,000: Space Marine 2 is here, appropriately dubbed the Decimation update, which adds in a new mode and more.

First up, that new mode! It's called Weekly Clash and it's for the competitive folks out there. "This new PvP shakes things up with the introduction of “Weekly Clash”, a new mode that brings unique new rules to Eternal War, like games restricted to a single class, a single weapon or even granting near-unlimited grenades," explains a Steam blog post. "Except more modifiers to be added in the future."

This update also introduces a new Chaos Siege sector, that new mode introduced last month, which adds in a "new playable sector bringing a renewed challenge between waves 11 and 15!" You'll also find six new heroic weapons in the armoury, like the omnissian axe, plasma incinerator and heavy bolter. This comes complete with some new heroic armour pieces, specifically four new helmets. On top of all of this, there's been a Vanguard rework: "Fight the enemies of Humanity with new ways to use your Grapnel Launcher! Attack cancellations, close-quarter kicks and a new Revenge mechanic make the Vanguard as bold and brutal as he’s ever been!"

Some other general tweaks have been made with this patch too. All PvP maps have seen the number and locations of ammo and equipment pickups adjusted, and conditions for the spawn position swap system have been improved. A level lock for the Absolute Siege and Absolute Stratagems mode has also been added; "The difficulty will be accessible to Classes that have reached level 25 or achieved Prestige at least once." And you'll also find that loading times and general connectivity should be a bit better!

#3727. World of Warcraft: Forever's best new enchantment has been quietly changed, leaving some casters on the back foot

As World of Warcraft: Forever players dived into the game, they quickly discovered a specific weapon enchant that took area of effect spells to a whole other level. Sadly, with a sudden hotfix last night, this particular use case for the enchant has been removed.

The enchantment in question was Revelation - a new addition to the game included as part of the new trade good reputations. What it does is simple: when you fail to deal a critical strike with a spell, the next spell hit is guaranteed to do so. What made this particularly powerful is that the buff also worked with continuous area of effect spells, meaning an early instance of the spell not crit-ing would result in the remaining damage hits all dealing critical damage.

So for example, let's say you're a druid casting the Hurricane spell. This is a channel spell with a total of 10 seconds of cast time. Every second, it deals damage. If the first instance of damage at the one second mark doesn't crit, the remaining nine instances of damage would all crit. This resulted in absurd amounts of damage, and made players of druids, warlocks, and mages very happy.

While strong enchantments are often pricey, this was notably cheap, due to the low-cost of resources used to create it and the low requirements to learn it. As such, people were spending a handful of gold for an early game enchantment that was being actively used all the way into the end game.

It was admittedly a tad too strong, and the effect triggered on AOE spells was almost certainly an unintended effect of the enchantment. Last night, the fun came to an end. Now, the effect is used up as intended in long-casted spells. So going back to the example given, if the first instance of damage on Hurricane doesn't crit, then the second one still will. However, this will use up the effect, and the third instance of damage will revert to regular ol' damage numbers. It also seems as though it Revelation can't trigger more than once during a single channeled spell.

This is the latest in a string of ongoing quickfire bug fixes and game adjustments being made to World of Warcraft: Forever. The devs have been continuously updating the game in an attempt to curb certain gold farms, following the discovery of a particularly lucrative Blackmaw Hold gold exploit. The dev team has expressed some interesting ideas for the game longterm, including a desire to kill best-in-slot gear.

BioWare "basically had no money left" before it was sold to private equity and then EA

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

EA wanted a World of Warcraft killer when it bought BioWare in 2007, according to Dragon Age producer Mark Darrah. But he says BioWare's MMO, Star Wars: The Old Republic, never did WoW numbers, and EA's higher-ups always "hated" it as a result.

BioWare was first acquired in 2005 by a private equity fund alongside Pandemic Studios, makers of the original Star Wars: Battlefront games, and packaged under a single holding company. While Darrah notes that he was a programmer in this era, and thus didn't have a great insight into BioWare's financial situation, his "understanding is that we basically had no money left. We needed money to continue to exist."

In an interview for podcast Pembridge TV, Darrah explains that BioWare intentionally "made games that were bigger than other people's games," and the studio continued to expand its scope by hiring more people. While the original studio, based in Edmonton, continued to develop single-player RPGs, BioWare opened a new studio in Austin, Texas to work on the massively multiplayer online game that would become Star Wars: The Old Republic. That, Darrah believes, is the true reason EA acquired BioWare.

"EA's always wanted everything to be a live service," Darrah says. "They just didn't use that language in the past. Back in the days before Destiny, the thing that was seen as the successful live service model was the MMO. Everyone wanted an MMO. World of Warcraft came out and totally redefined the space. Everyone wanted a World of Warcraft killer. I mean, it was Star Wars. Surely it could be the World of Warcraft killer."

So, as part of a package deal with BioWare's single-player RPG studio in Edmonton and Pandemic, EA bought its potential WoW killer. Darrah recalls speculating on why EA was laying out so much money for the acquisition: "It's like, 'okay, well, they really want Star Wars: The Old Republic. They want the MMO. They obviously want [Battlefront].' Then it's like, 'oh, and they're getting BioWare Edmonton.' For me, and for many people in Edmonton at the time of the acquisition, it looked like EA was buying Star Wars: The Old Republic and Pandemic and getting BioWare Edmonton as a side effect."

Of course, Pandemic ended up being an early casualty of the acquisition, as EA shut it down in 2009. "Star Wars: The Old Republic more than paid for itself eventually, but it took a really long time. The probably single best return on investment that EA got was BioWare Edmonton, even though it seemed like we were just an afterthought."

But while The Old Republic eventually made back EA's investment the publisher resented the game for failing to meet its lofty expectations at launch.

Weekly digests, tales from the communities you love, and more

"EA hated SWTOR from the beginning," Darrah says, pointing particular blame at then-EA studios boss Patrick Söderlund. "They wanted it really bad, but all indication – and someone from Austin could probably speak to this more than me – it always seemed to me like they wanted it gone pretty much from the instant it launched and didn't hit its numbers. They never wanted to invest in it. They always wanted to push it out of the conversation. They talked about pulling people off of it for a really long time. But it did generate money."

Still, Darrah suggests that the exact same thing happened when BioWare made its next live-service game, Anthem. By that time, MMOs were looking like old news. "If you're not WoW are going to come out, and then they're going to go free-to- play and then they're going to slowly decay away," Darrah says. But he puts EA's perspective like this: "We don't want that. We want Destiny. Destiny's making so much money."

Then, of course, Anthem came out, had its moment, and slowly decayed away. The irony is that, at this point, The Old Republic – which is still running and receiving new content – is set to outlast Anthem, Destiny, and even BioWare itself.

"Maybe most corporations are incapable of learning those lessons," Darrah laments.

#3725. HARK THE GHOUL is a Victorian gothic dungeon crawler RPG that features a trench-coat-wearing rat man who wants to sell you rats a la counterfeit watches

I'm a simple person. I see an anthropomorphic rat man who opens up his trench coat that is filled with regular rats in the same manner as one would with counterfeit watches in a trailer for a video game, I add it to my wishlist. There really isn't much I need in life, but that certainly fulfills those needs. And it's exactly what HARK THE GHOUL is offering, an action-adventure, dungeon crawler RPG set in a weird and nasty Victorian gothic city with an emphasis on free exploration.

Now, I appreciate not all of you will be as immediately convinced by trench coat wearing rat men, so let's have a deeper gander at the game together. Exploration really does seem to be the key thing here, not just in terms of going wherever you want, more or less when you want, but how you get about. For example, say there's an annoying gap you want to cross. Use a magical spell to summon a crate, then lob it in front of you, and cast some icey magic to freeze it into place, thereby creating a new platform for you to hop onto. Looks like nice and systemic stuff!

HARK THE GHOUL releases 👉JANUARY 21st, 2027!!!👈 Our action-adventure RPG built around freeform exploration lets you loose in a dark Victorian city full of secrets to uncover and ravenous monsters to defeat! Coming to Steam, Switch 1, Switch 2, PS5 and Xbox Series![image or embed]

This extends to the combat, which faces you against odd automatons, infected foes and nasty beasties. You can perform quite silly tricks like using your shovel to dig up a rock and chuck that at a baddie, or you can use your magic to conjure up an explosive crate which you then kick at an enemy, blasting it with a shotgun. It appears to almost be an RPG by way of the immersive sim; there's no correct way to go about the game, only the way you find most fun. Though maybe that's dredging up the debate around what an immersive sim is…

Either way, I'm just tickled pink by HARK THE GHOUL, which also pits you as a mothman-type figure who's just emerged from their cocoon. Delightful! And it just got a release date too: January 21st, 2027. That's only a couple of months away, obviously, but if you can't wait that long then there's a demo you can check out on Steam. Or, you know, just throw it a wishlist! Offering it some support either way seems like a nice idea.

#3724. Why did Rockstar Games make empathy a key mechanic in GTA 6? "Because it's fun" says head of development Rob Nelson

That, and parts of RDR2 became "too hard to ignore or walk away from".

There's been plenty of chatter about Grand Theft Auto 6's 'honour system', so to speak, implemented here via what the game calls your Criminal Profile.

Our own Dom just wrote that they prefer to turn its notifications off, for instance, in favour of fully soaking into the immersion. Personally I quite like the pop-ups - I find the act of figuring out systems and how they're manipulated almost as fun as the games they're a part of. And pop-ups or no, the fact that GTA 6 can arguably be portrayed as 'rewarding' empathy and 'discouraging' the series' famous rampages of mass violence has sparked a fair bit of debate.

Some of that is genuinely interesting - I'm dubious as to whether that's really what this system is doing, for a start. Is it incentivising and disincentivising certain in-game behaviour, or just putting a label on it? And then, actually: does the act of labelling "psycho" behaviour alone actually become a disincentivising factor in itself?

Either way, until now Rockstar hasn't said a great deal about why, exactly, this system - seen by some as one that builds empathy into GTA's chaotic world - was implemented in the first place. But during an interview I had with Rob Nelson, Rockstar Games' head of development, just before GTA 6's launch earlier this month, a little more on that came to light.

A little context is necessary here: Nelson's response was actually following a question I had about the overall approach to design that Rockstar took, and how its wider themes and intentions came about. As a part of that, he turned to this system - and how, in a way, it exists here because of the work the studio simply didn't want to leave behind after Red Dead Redemption 2.

Nelson explained that this all began when the team was in the early phase of exploring what type of game GTA 6 would be, in 2015 and 2016, while much of the studio was still working full-tilt on RDR2 - a game which itself didn't release until late 2018. The team was looking to "build up the sophistication of the NPC population, and also allow for more player choice than we had [before], and more options in terms of the way you interact with the world beyond just violence," Nelson told me.

The idea would be that "it's still a world of violence - but you could threaten somebody by aiming a gun at them and just robbing them, and they have a chance to comply. So you don't have to beat them to death to get their money." Ideas that were "simple things" in principle, he said, "but they create a lot more work in terms of development of the sophistication of the systems."

Then, as systems were gradually implemented, it became a question of "trying to marry up what you're doing in the open world with who we're saying you are in the narrative - more than we had, I would say, previously, in Red Dead 2." It's here where the system now referred to as the Criminal Profile started to form.

The thinking turned to "the nature of 'honour', which wasn't always a part of it" with Red Dead Redemption 2, Nelson continued, "but became part of it as we were working on this story and finding that the 'redemption arc' didn't feel so good when it was foisted upon you - and feelings that we had playing Red Dead sort of early on." (Those feelings, primarily, were around getting you to invest in a gang led by Dutch Van der Linde, who was fundamentally unlikable from the off - or plain "crazy", as Nelson put it. The implementation of more player choices and agency was part of Rockstar's way to build investment in Arthur, even as he followed Dutch.)

That meant moving the choices away from key story moments, where many games tend to put them. Instead, Rockstar built a system that ran alongside the story via smaller, moment-to-moment choices you might make. "We tried to take all of those off the main flow and make them optional. So again, they're a choice."

"Usually they involve some form of slight sacrifice or more effort on the part of the player," he added. The hope, then, was that you as a player would both "feel something", and ultimately also feel "you got the outcome that you deserved."

That was the initial thinking behind this kind of system as a whole. Coming to GTA 6, it then combined with a wider desire to "evolve" Grand Theft Auto as both the team's storytelling and the available technology matured. "You're thinking about story and character set, but we're also thinking about what we want to do with GTA as a series, and how you want to evolve it," Nelson said.

"I think as the resolution goes up, it sort of asks different new questions," he continued. "As the resolution goes up, you want the sophistication of the experience to go up, and obviously the sophistication of the mechanics. So it just naturally flowed that we give players choices to interact with the world beyond just violence, beyond just 'down the barrel of a gun', because it's fun."

"It's fun for some people like myself to just sort of role-play in the world, and be in the world, and restraint becomes something you hadn't thought about," he continued. That tied back into the more sophisticated NPCs and reactions the team were making.

"If you think about the NPCs, even back to [GTA] 5, you would draw a weapon - first of all, they didn't react if you drew an invisible shotgun out of nowhere, or a rocket launcher," he said. "They don't react unless you aim it, and then they flee in terror, and you're just sort of this demigod stomping through the world, you know? And that's fun, but for how long?

"The team then started thinking of ways to build a bit more sustained enjoyment from it. "What if you can't do that?" Nelson continued. What if, instead of whipping an RPG out of nowhere, "you have to call your car. You have to pop a car trunk and get it, and now I'm walking, and now people are noticing, but they're sort of sidling away, and it's more believable. And then they're still fleeing in terror, but then there's people who also have guns, and they're shooting at you, or you try to hold somebody up and they pull a gun, or they grab it, and then you have to deal with them.

"And then, he continued, "you choose. You're trying to jack somebody off a motorcycle, and they pull a gun on you, and you have to blow their head off and it's like, 'You shouldn't have made me do that!' And so then it has more meaning, and it's more funny in a way when it's a little bit more pointed. And you can still go on those rampages and basically smash your Criminal Profile until it breaks and then you enter this irredeemable state, which basically says 'I reject your criminal profile system! I don't want it.'"

That Irredeemable profile level, for what it's worth, was another element born of Red Dead Redemption 2. "We had that with Red Dead, where people would sort of have low honour, and then 'greet' their way back up to high honour. And so this was an attempt of sorts of [making something] for people that just want to go crazy and almost opt out of the system. They can opt out of it - and you can also turn off the notifications in the system."

It's notable, in fact, just how interlinked the thinking was with GTA 6 and Red Dead Redemption 2. As Nelson put it at one point: "There was maybe more emotional resonance in the story of RDR2 than we had had, certainly in a GTA before. So we liked that idea." What Rockstar did with GTA 6 was then in a way a natural next step. "We didn't necessarily come to GTA 6 going: 'We must have emotional resonance,' but all of those things combine. It's more that those systems and that element of player choice and agency, and the way that affected the narrative, was a hard thing to ignore and walk away from."

We'll have much more like this from our interview with Nelson very soon, so do look out for that on Eurogamer over the coming days. In the meantime, we've a handy guide explaining exactly how GTA 6's Criminal Profile system works and how to change, raise, or lower that profile if you're in need of a deep dive into how it all really works.

#3723. Your mothership is a giant pinball machine and your ball is its defence system in Appulse, a top-down roguelite shooter that's out now

Pinball remains such an intoxicating game because it's one where you have to constantly be on your toes. As the tiny metal sphere bats about the place, it's down to you to hit it at just the right time so as to keep racking up points upon points. It's a game of skill as much as it is luck. It is also incredibly silly, which is why I'm so tickled by Appulse, a sci-fi pinball roguelite top-down shooter that launched today wherein your ball is actually the main defence system on your spaceship.

Yes! This is also silly! Especially considering the semi-realistic sci-fi vibe of it all. It encourages me to wonder who in this world looked at pinball and thought, "yes, this is the optimum method of defending our ship from invading robots." And I love this fictional character for such a thought!

At its most basic function, Appulse works exactly as you'd expect from a pinball game, in that you shoot your ball, or ship in this case, and hit those flappers to keep it in the air, so to speak. Accept the key difference is your ball/ship has guns that you use to shoot the aforementioned invading robots, while also doubling up as an extra method for control. Need to right a bad hit? Shoot your shot and you'll fly off in the opposite direction.

I've seen this in other digital pinball games before, but that's not a knock, I can't imagine having to manage all this shooting without some semblance of control. The roguelite mechanics sound pretty nifty too. You can get perks like extra recoil when firing, which obviously will aid you in staying in control. Or you may unlock the ability to slow down time. Builds sound pretty flexible! And overall it just looks like a neat little time. If Appulse takes your fancy, then as mentioned it's available to pick up on Steam now.

The Wicker cast has been feeding into innuendo pretty much since all the horny reviews dropped for the 2026 movie release. Having seen the movie in theaters myself, I have to say I wholeheartedly approve. So, I guess I shouldn’t have been surprised when lead Olivia Colman pulled a wicker, penis-shaped vibrator out of her purse during a recent appearance, but I was! I wonder if Alexander Skarsgård knows she has this homage to his member on her person at any given time?

Wicker’s been landing some Oscar buzz, particularly in its Craft categories, but the leads have been out and about helping with the push in recent days. Lead Olivia Colman was recently out supporting Wicker when she signed on for British Vogue’s “What’s in my Bag” segment, which nearly always features an interesting array of random objects. In this case, one of the first things the actress pulled out was a Wicker vibrator, no joke.

She said fans might be “surprised” she’s just carrying around the wicker contraption, and joked she's “going to say it’s a lipstick" before also pulling out some Kitkats and Twix bars. See the surprise moment, below.

A post shared by British Vogue (@britishvogue)

I certainly didn’t see the wicker vibrator coming, but I do have questions. Namely, that doesn’t look like the very uncomfortable prosthetics Alexander Skarsgård was wearing on set. So, like where does one get a wicker vibrator? Did a fan make that and give it to her? Does she keep that in her bag all the time, or was this just tossed in to throw Wicker into the conversation? Again, does her co-star know she's carrying this around?

Any way you look at this, it's very funny, and as she succinctly put it:

If you’re offended by what I have in my bag, I don’t care.

With a Wicker Oscars push, anything is possible. Honestly I'd be down for some Best Actor/Actress noms. Colman and Skarsgård are so good in the movie and when I saw it in a theater full of women, the crowd was rowdy and having fun with the premise, which was so cheeky and unexpected. Even the merch for this movie follows suit! I mean, the popcorn bucket needs its own intimacy coordinator!

Anyway, I had the best time watching this movie, and I’ve totally enjoyed the way the two actors have been promoting the film in the time since, which includes but is not limited to Skarsgård’s feet (likely) ending up on wikifeet. This is the movie that really just keeps on giving and giving, and it just hit VOD so you can now even watch it from the comfort of your own home. I suggest you do so before awards season!

Steam isn't running an official Black Friday fest—it says so right here in this update, "Steam isn't running an official Black Friday fest"—but plenty of game developers have marked their stuff down to take advantage of the big sale season, and so Valve is helping them all out a bit by "dressing up" its Discounts and Events page in the appropriate seasonal garb.

Is there a little bit of wink wink, nudge nudge to that 'not a Black Friday fest' business? Hey, maybe.

In fair play, though, Steam traditionally hasn't run Black Friday sales, because its Autumn Sale was always happening at the same time. The realignment of seasonal sales in 2025 changed that, however, leaving a hole that was filled by the first-ever Steam Black Friday Sale last year.

Valve has other priorities this year, though, which could explain the absence (wink wink, nudge nudge) of an official Black Friday event on Steam in 2026. In September, Valve announced changes to Steam's Discounts and Events page to make it prettier and more personalized, and it said in today's update that Black Friday is "the perfect time to share the updates we've been working on to make the Discounts & Events page a better experience altogether."

With that all cleared up, I'll say that the Black Friday non-fest page is definitely an eye-catcher, and it will be interesting to see how Valve puts this section of Steam to work in the future. If it's treated like an 'almost a Steam sale' that never really ends, I have to think that developers and gamers alike will benefit—at least until we all get used to it and Valve has to figure out some new way to tweak the formula.

For now, since we're here, let's check out some deals:

And here's one other difference between actual Steam sales and the Black Friday non-event: Valve said the Black Friday decor will come off the Discounts and Events page on November 30, but the discounts themselves all have separate end dates. The Divinity: Original Sin 2 sale, for instance, also ends on November 30, but Outer Wilds will stay marked down until December 5, and the Esoteric Ebb deal will be valid until December 7.

#3719. Dark fantasy and sudoku fuse together in unholy matrimony in Dungoku, a dungeon crawling twist on the classic puzzle game

My only question is, is it a soft g like in dungeon, or a hard g like that guy from Dragon Ball?

Maths is not my strong suit, I make no secret of this, so when I come face to face with something like sudoku I will admit to recoiling in fear at having to confront this issue. Numbers don't make sense to me at the best of times, and now I have to figure out the specific placements of them whereby each number can only be used once per section, and each column and row have to all contain numbers one through nine? Terrifying! No, thanks, I'd much rather do the exact same thing but with, I don't know, skeletons and ghouls and the like. Which, conveniently, is more or less what Dungoku offers, a genre mashup of dungeon crawling and sudoku with a retro dark fantasy vibe.

Okay, it's not exactly the same. You don't crawl the dungeons in the typical fashion here as it leans heavily towards the puzzle side of things. Maps come in different, grid-based shapes and sizes, but to start they are mostly void of enemies. It's predominantly up to you to place enemies, or sometimes chests, in specific squares, all of which have their own rules that you must follow, with a set number that need to be placed on the map.

For example, one enemy may have a requirement that it is adjacent to a zombie in the same room. Another might need to be placed in a dead end. Others, like an owl creature, can only share a room with itself or other animals. So, it's different from sudoku in that each puzzle features changing enemies that have to be placed, as opposed to always needing to follow the same basic rules. It seems like a clever spin on the classic puzzle! Plus there's loot to be acquired that improves your stats and thereby your chance of survival (making a mistake in placement results in, obviously, getting hurt; this is still a dungeon crawler!).

In total there's apparently over 100 "hand-crafted dungeons to explore," and more than 20 monsters to take on, so it sounds like there's some good potential for interesting puzzle combinations. I also like the specific mention of "human composed music," certainly makes it sound like AI wasn't involved, and lord almighty I hope that to be true! No release date attached to this one just yet, but you can wishlist it on Steam in the meantime.

#3718. EA is resurrecting a dead commentator with AI for EA Sports FC 27, years after his last appearance in a FIFA game

"He was the very first voice of our game - so we really wanted to do him justice and bring him back."

EA Sports FC 27 is using gen-AI to digitally recreate the voice of veteran football commentator John Motson - the FIFA video game series' first ever real-world announcer who died in 2023.

John Motson commentated on hundreds of football games over the course of five different decades, starting in the 1970s. The English commentator then became the mainstay voice of EA's dominant football simulation series, beginning with FIFA 96 all the way up until FIFA 2005, when the publisher decided to go in a different direction.

But EA's now decided to digitally resurrect Motson - or, at least, his incredibly recognisable voice - with permission from his family. An update with Motson's voice will go live on 26th November. "There was no way we would have moved forward with this in any way, shape or form if they weren't fully on board," senior game designer director Mat Prior said in a statement given to the BBC earlier today.

"At the outset we wanted to pay tribute to to Motty as the commentator and as this emotional connection - he was the very first voice of our game - so we really wanted to do him justice and bring him back," Prior added, explaining that Motson's posthumous role in the game is being handled with a mixture of previously recorded voice lines and AI. EA supposedly went down the AI route since it doesn't have recordings of Motson commentating over newer, more fresh faced footballers.

Fred Motson said it "means an awful lot" to hear his dad's voice in the game again, and he reckons his dad was "always really keen to get involved in these kinds of projects," even if he wasn't the most technologically savvy person. EA said it had paid the family for the rights to use Motson's voice and likeness.

Save Our Voices Now founder Peter Caulfield - who campaigns for the government to regulate the use of generative AI voice cloning tech - told the BBC he wasn't comfortable with the project. "In life or in death, unless you have specifically agreed to it, AI cloning of any kind should not be allowed," he said. "Being a family member shouldn't automatically give you that right either." He doesn't have a problem with actors consenting to AI voice replication while they're still alive, however.

A Japanese acting union recently fought back against this very same practice by proposing new guidelines that would stop the replication of dead actors' voices without their permission.

Generative AI has been widely controversial in the games industry for other reasons, too. In recent months, there's been a huge impact on smaller game developers who are worried that their games could be cloned by AI copycats and some who have had to delay their release dates because of Steam's growing approvals backlog.

"The Grounds comes across as a frippery, Ultimate Team rumbles ever on, but FC 27 brings meaningful changes to the fluidity and speed of play. Given that its practical football-game monopoly is more or less unchallenged, EA could do a lot less than this," Josh Wise wrote in Eurogamer's EA Sports FC 27 review.

2026 was a big year for friendslop, but 2025 was its breakout year. That's thanks in large part to Peak, which not only drew in millions of players, but helped establish a new genre after its developers happily leaned into the new term, despite its less-than-complimentary description. But it was actually 2020 that might have been the most important year for friendslop.

That's according to Petter Henriksson, CEO of Landfall Games, which was one half of Peak alongside Aggro Crab Studios. Speaking about the growth of cooperative games in the latest issue of Edge Magazine, he says that during the pandemic "gaming became more acceptable as a social endeavour," and that it found mainstream acceptance as "how you create social contact with your friends."

But that came at something of a cost. During those lockdowns, Henriksson says "we spent a lot of years playing multiplayer together and someone always had to lose." The problem there, he points out, is that "you don't want to play with all your friends in your game and you lose." And that's because, as he so cunningly puts it: "Losing feels terrible."

Now, before the inevitable joke about why nobody told my League of Legends friends that, I should point out that Henriksson is making a wider point about game design, rather than simply telling you you'd rather win. If the point of playing the game is to spend time with friends, forcing someone to lose isn't necessarily conducive to keeping that group playing. 'Friendslop' maintains stakes, but its generally collaborative approach means that you all win as a team, or all lose as a team - rather than making any one person do better than everyone else.

Henriksson's ideas are hardly new - the idea of friendslop has been pretty mainstream since Among Us was a breakout hit in 2020 - but it's interesting to see this philosophy put forward in such a simple way. Elsewhere in the feature, we hear from the teams behind REPO, Big Walk, and even Wardogs, but it's Henriksson who once again makes an excellent point about how the genre has changed. Peak kicked off a huge swathe of friendly co-op titles, but in doing so it massively raised the bar: "If you make a friendslop game today, it has to be a lot better than it had to be when we did it."

#3716. "Does changing where games run cross a legal line?" Microsoft-owned Github ask in now-deleted post celebrating GTA 6's effect on PC port-focused PS5 emulator

"GTA 6 is finally here, sparking one of the biggest weeks in gaming and open source on GitHub"

'Yay, GTA 6 is out on consoles and lots of people are playing it' is a fairly harmless thing to say. Unless you're, I dunno, a development platform mentioning that in a post celebrating the recent success of a PS5 emulator used for making unofficial PC ports of console games. You know, the sorts of unofficial PC ports vibecoders and proper coders having been scrambling to make of GTA 6 since its Xbox executable was allegedly leaked. The sorts of unofficial PC ports publishers like Rockstar tend to quickly move to have taken down.

"GTA 6 is finally here, sparking one of the biggest weeks in gaming and open source on Github," read a Github tweet screengabbed by Kotaku before it was deep sixed. "The repo AnyPS5 has passed 58K stars since its August launch, rewriting PS5 executables to run on Windows and Linux. Does changing where games run cross a legal line? Share your take. Happy GTA VImas!"

A video alongside the post seems to have dug the hole even deeper. "The project rewrites a game's executable so Windows and Linux can run it directly," a presenter cheerily declared. "Performance seems to be the main issue for users wanting to run GTA 6, with one contributor telling the project's community to lock in and get their agents to help if they need to." From there, the "big question" of whether it's actually legal to change where and how your games run was posed by Github.

And now their tweet is deleted. Here was the text. https://t.co/kNbmmPCGdf

One can only imagine how raised the eyebrows of Rockstar affiliated lawyers may have become if they read the post before Github yanked it.

Another big question posed a lot recently is whether the threat of bodged PC recreations based on the alleged leaked executable may lead Rockstar to narrow the gap between GTA 6's console release and its eventual Windows launch, which reports have previously claimed is planned for the opening months of next year. You know, because the company and publishers Take-Two presumably don't want to risk the sales of an official port being undercut by an unofficial one, no matter the degree of impact that might actually have (my presumption would be the official port would still rake in a fortune).

Given the reception their baffling AnyPS5 post received, I doubt Github'll be providing any more commentary on the rush to unofficially port GTA 6 and the debate as to when it might hit PC officially.

#3715. Original Devil May Cry and Bayonetta director Hideki Kamiya really wants Konami to let him make a "truly insane" Castlevania game

Action game maestro Hideki Kamiya really wants to make a new Castlevania game with publisher Konami.

The long-time developer best known for his work in the director's chair on a host of beloved games - Bayonetta, Resident Evil 2, Okami, Devil May Cry and The Wonderful 101 included - recently published a new video to his personal YouTube account. While the video was first recorded last year, it does give us some hints on what Kamiya is interested in making after his in-development Okami sequel wraps up.

Perhaps the most noteworthy tidbit came from Kamiya advocating to make a new game in Konami's vampiric action-adventure series. "We'll definitely make Castlevania. If you let us work on it, we can make something truly insane, so just contact us and we'll be at your service," Kamiya said. (Thanks, Automaton!)

Kamiya presumably has his hands full with Capcom's Okami 2, which is currently in production at the director's newfound independent studio Clovers. Needless to say, any potential Kamiya-led Castlevania game will likely need to wait in a coffin for a while more.

In the meantime, it's not like Castlevania has remained dormant and defanged. Earlier this year, Konami promised that "numerous new products around Castlevania" are in the pipeline. While new games weren't explicitly confirmed, it's safe to assume Konami would be interested in hearing pitches from outside devs. Kamiya can stay hopeful knowing that Evil Empire just dropped another gorgeous, aggressive action-platformer in the series.

"Like Rose herself, the game is earnest, intelligent, and capable of brilliance. But, mimicking its protagonist, it is also awkward, and unable to fully come to terms with its own unique identity in the shadow of its over-bearing legacy," Dom wrote in Eurogamer's Castlevania: Belmont's Curse review. "By no means is Belmont's Curse a bad game, I just think Evil Empire sunk its teeth a bit too deep into something it wasn't quite ready to consume."

This isn't the first time Kamiya has publicly expressed interest in reviving older games, either. He recently said he's "100% serious" about bringing back Scalebound, his cancelled Xbox One exclusive.

Blizzard's latest patch prevents Alterac Valley from being a glorified reputation farm.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Despite being set in the past, WoW: Forever is an attempt to capture the spirit of the old game by injecting it with new quirks that challenge new and returning players alike to approach it differently than any other version of the MMO. This is why familiar old dungeons can drop new loot, like an armor set that turns you into a snake.

Blizzard has said that its goal is to "unsolve" the game as best it can so players don't settle into the same routines they're used to. This is especially true for min-maxed strategies that threaten to suck the fun out of enjoying the game, or "the journey", as Blizzard likes to call it.

It's a lofty goal that can't be achieved without persistently fiddling with the knobs that encourage players to do one thing over another—which is the very thing that differentiates WoW: Forever from WoW Classic.

This week, Blizzard stepped in to fix a problem that was brewing in its 40-player MOBA-esque PvP mode Alterac Valley. Players were avoiding PvP altogether, turning it into a glorified reputation farm.

"We’ve seen that players in Alterac Valley were frequently completing the battleground without capturing the objectives, so we’ve made some adjustments to incentivize a focus on the objectives rather than rushing to kill the enemy faction’s general," community manager Kaivax wrote.

The patch basically broke a popular 'zerg' strategy where one side rushed to end the match as fast as possible by beefing up the NPC defenders that stood in their way. Blizzard shifted some of the reputation and honor you'd normally get from killing the generals to the other objectives so players are encouraged to engage with the whole mode.

But, as I've seen with changes like this in the past few weeks, many players are upset that they can't just spam it for the rewards, and that others have already reaped the benefits of the old strategy. There are people in Reddit threads doing the math to highlight how much efficiency has been lost (it doesn't seem like much) and questioning the point of doing Alterac Valley at all.

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

While I sympathize with not wanting to do something that feels like a chore, it's a far worse problem to have an entire part of the game flattened into an AFK farm. Alterac Valley is supposed to feel like a large-scale war where you look at a big map and choose what objectives are worth fighting over as you try to weaken the enemy forces. The loot you get from maxing out your reputation with the associated factions is meant to be a reward for putting in the effort to learn what it takes to win.

The whole pitch for WoW: Forever is that it's not going to ditch everything with a new expansion every few years. Numbers can be tweaked down the line if the reputation grind is too much of a slog, but the mode should be fun to play so it's not treated like a box to check off in your character's journey. An inert PvP mode ruins the spirit of the MMO far more than a slightly longer reputation grind does.

I think this is a good example of a healthy change that shows Blizzard is committed to protecting core parts of the experience from becoming a treadmill that nobody enjoys. WoW: Forever's strengths are the ways it encourages you to participate in systems that aren't there to fill progression bars. As Harvey said in his WoW: Forever review, "Forever is proof that old-school MMO design deserves a second chance," and that requires taking a stance on what the game is and isn't meant to be.

#3713. Drone Pilots have come to Cyber Knights: Flashpoint, the stealth tactics game's "most complex" class yet, alongside a pet system and the promise of "assassin cats"

How dare you accuse me of being a friendless loser! I have loads of friends! Their names are R2-D2 and Clippy and Arnold and Rosie the Maid. They all live in my rucksack, ready and waiting should I need somebody to dupe a security guard or fill the air around me with explosive chaff. All except Clippy, that is. He's too chonky to stuff in a bag, which can make for tricky mission extractions, but he compensates for that with his generous selection of *voice drops six octaves* FULLY LOADED AUTOCANNONS.

With friends like these, who needs human allies? It's time to play stealth tactics sim Cyber Knights: Flashpoint the way it was meant to be played: skulking in a hole while buzzing, clanking mechabastards cleanse the map of any and all defenders. Don't spare the lead, Rosie. You were not built to understand mercy.

Let's try that again: wireheady heist-me-do Cyber Knights: Flashpoint has received a major update adding a new player class, the Drone Pilot, billed by developers Trese Brothers as "the most complex" and among the most "flexible" of the game's Neuromantic vocations. The Drone Pilot arrives alongside a new pet system they'll be using down the road for "warhunds and assassin cats". Right now, though, the only "pets" at your disposal appear to be those drones. Here's what they're good for: "jamming enemy systems, disabling security devices in passing, hijacking enemy drones to turn on their own side, or trailing fields of shredding nano-chaff and squad-boosting support zones wherever the drone flies."

Drones come in three types, light (fast and best for stealthy support), medium (a mix of support and combat-oriented), and heavy (flying forts and/or stomping murder mechs). Light or medium drones are deployed from your backpack, and auto-extract when you do, no matter where they are. Heavy drones deploy alongside you at mission start, and have to be within nine metres of you when you extract, potentially trapping you on the map. Each drone chassis has its own weapon and armour setup, plus a choice of modules that grant Talents (abilities).

While rolling a Drone Pilot might seem like an opportunity to forgo any and all squidgy organic accomplices, the big catch is that Drone Pilots and their mecha mates share action and movement points. While using the Full Pilot talent, you can transfer AP to a drone so that it can move and fight like a full separate character. While using the Auto-Pilot talent, you'll only share bonus MP. There's also the option to multi-class, with Trese Brothers noting that "dipping into another class can significantly increase their flexibility or buff their personal abilities with just a few talents from an alternate tree".

As for how you'll get your hands on the Drone Pilot class, their costs make them a poor fit for teams with a power level below three, so they aren't among the New Game options. You'll be able to recruit them in the Underworld Hub and also, turn characters into drone pilots once you acquire a Pilot Wire cybernetic implant and the requisite cyber surgery. The Pilot Wire uses up a Deep Brain slot, making the class incompatible with the Hacker or Wireghost classes. Beyond that, you can reach out to a smuggler or broker to get access to new and better drones and pilot cybernetics.

Pettable killdroids aside, Trese Brothers are continuing work on Cyber Knight's mod support. The latest update adds features for official language translation mods and Attribute bonus tweaking, alongside expanded Legwork options. They're also labouring away on a modkit preview project of some kind. Read more on Steam.

New to Cyber Knights? Congratulations on digesting all the above gibberish about weaponised WALL-Es. I can only assume you read the whole thing in hopes of further talk of "assassin cats", but alas, Trese Brothers are maintaining an ominous silence. Instead, here is what Nic Reuben (RPS in peace) had to say about the game in our 2025 review: "Don't let its initial cyber-posturing and sheer amount of systems intimidate you. Cyber Knights: Flashpoint is wider than it is oppressively deep, while still being rich enough to offer up some excellently tense and entertaining stealth tactics."

#3712. The Fable reboot had to look beyond Lionhead's RPG trilogy because games like The Witcher 3 "became the gold standard"

Developer Playground Games had to look beyond Lionhead's original run of Fable games when rebooting the classic fantasy series, and it's all thanks to games like The Witcher 3, which changed what many players expect from their big RPGs and set a new "gold standard."

The upcoming Fable reboot is finally ending its decade-long development journey soon. Playground Games had to set up an entirely new team to work on its fairytale revival, so Fable's production wasn't quite as smooth sailing as the studio's consistently excellent Forza Horizon series, for example.

Asked about what's changed during that time, in an interview with GamesIndustry.biz, studio founder and general manager Ralph Fulton named technological advancements as a biggie, but the impact of other games was perhaps even greater.

"In 2015, The Witcher 3 redefined what an open-world action RPG looks like and became the gold standard," Fulton said. "And after that bar was raised, the Assassin's Creed franchise changed into this more modern iteration with Origins, Odyssey, and Valhalla, and became like a quasi-RPG."

"All of these games continue to reset player expectations," he continued. Millions of players suddenly had certain expectations about what their big-budget, open-world role-playing games should look like. So, Playground couldn't pull inspiration from Fable and Fable alone.

"I think looking only to the original Fable trilogy for inspiration would leave us lacking in terms of what the modern audience, the modern marketplace, expects," Fulton added.

Still, Playground's Fable is drawing most heavily from Lionhead's Fable. Fulton specifically mentions the game's signature British wit and in-flux morality system as examples. Then there's also the spontaneous life sim elements that "none of our competitors do," according to Fulton. "It's a totally Fable thing, the social simulation and economic simulation. Okay, there are games that have economic simulations, but they're not in [our] RPG category. Fable is unique in that it's almost like a life sim in terms of genre."

Raising four separate families and becoming the entire map's benevolent landlord was one of the funnest parts of Fable back in the day, alongside those sometimes silly characters. Seeing next year's Fable lean into those systemic choices, and having Albion's NPCs react to them more believably, could give this one a very long shelf life.

It's hard to imagine Christmas without Buddy the Elf, but Hollywood wasn't convinced the movie would work.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

With the holiday season upon us and the 2026 movie calendar winding down, there are a handful of the best Christmas movies I return to every December, and Elf is pretty much guaranteed to make the list. Will Ferrell running around New York City in yellow tights, eating spaghetti covered in candy and screaming about Santa Claus has become as much a part of the holidays as putting up the tree. According to one of the movie's stars, Hollywood wasn't exactly convinced it had a future Christmas classic on its hands back in 2003.

Andy Richter, who played Morris in the Jon Favreau-directed comedy, recently reflected on the making of Elf and explained why the movie was considered something of a gamble. Speaking with People while promoting his new book, Elf: Unwrapped, which he co-wrote with Aaron Karo, Richter said the movie's eventual success makes it easy to forget just how uncertain things were when production began.

It was a risky movie, and nobody thinks about that because it’s now a classic, but at the time there was nobody that was aching to make a movie with Will Ferrell as the star or with Jon Favreau as the director, for that matter.

Considering Will Ferrell himself had doubts when he first tried on Buddy's iconic costume, I can understand why some studio executives might have been nervous. At the time, the SNL alum was best known for his work on Saturday Night Live, where he'd spent seven seasons establishing himself as one of the show's biggest stars. He'd appeared in movies like Old School and Zoolander, but he hadn't yet proven he could carry a major studio comedy as its leading man.

Favreau, meanwhile, had directed the 2001 comedy Made, but he was still relatively inexperienced behind the camera. According to Richter, the studio was taking a chance on both men. He added:

They were rolling the dice with this movie and it really paid off.

It's funny to think about now, considering Ferrell went on to become one of the biggest comedy stars of the 2000s, while Favreau would eventually direct Iron Man, helping launch the Marvel Cinematic Universe. He's also had a major hand in shaping the modern Star Wars franchise with The Mandalorian. But back in 2003, the idea of giving a relatively untested leading man a Christmas comedy about a grown man raised by elves probably sounded pretty ridiculous on paper. And considering some of the behind-the-scenes stories about making Elf, it's remarkable how well everything came together. It is a ridiculous premise. That's a big part of why I love it.

Richter also credited the combination of Ferrell's comedic instincts and Favreau's approach to storytelling for making the movie work. Interestingly, though, the movie’s star recently addressed the longstanding rumors about his relationship with Favreau during the production. It seems there's still plenty to learn about what went into making this particular Christmas classic. As for Richter, he told the outlet that the film succeeds because:

The combination of their two sensibilities, which we go into in the book, that really made it work because it’s funny, but also has a lot of heart.

I think that's a pretty accurate assessment. Ferrell gets to be completely absurd as Buddy, whether he's congratulating a coffee shop for having the world's best cup of coffee or trying to navigate a revolving door. Yet the movie also gives us a genuinely sweet story about a guy looking for his father and trying to find somewhere he belongs.

James Caan's performance as Walter Hobbs deserves some credit here, too. His perpetually irritated reaction to Buddy's enthusiasm makes their relationship work, and without that dynamic, I don't think the movie would have nearly the same emotional payoff. Whatever reservations Hollywood had about the project, audiences certainly didn't share them once it arrived in theaters.

According to The Numbers, Elf opened to more than $31 million during its first weekend in November 2003. It has since earned approximately $234 million worldwide, including revenue from subsequent theatrical releases. That's a pretty impressive return for a movie with a reported $32 million production budget.

The movie was successful enough that Hollywood naturally wanted another one, though Ferrell has since explained why he walked away from a potentially lucrative Elf sequel.

More than two decades later, it's difficult to imagine the holiday season without Buddy the Elf. The movie remains a favorite among families, and people are still finding new things to appreciate about it, including one particularly interesting question about Buddy's journey from the North Pole to New York City.

I find it interesting that a movie nobody could guarantee would succeed has become something people practically schedule their Christmas celebrations around. Ferrell has made plenty of successful comedies since, and Favreau's career has gone places nobody could have predicted in 2003.

There's something special about Elf. Considering how many Christmas movies come and go without making much of an impression, I suspect the people who took that gamble are pretty happy they did.

Elf is streaming with a Hulu subscription.

#3710. "A new era" for Vermintide 2 modding dawneth, as Fatshark release powerful new tools for custom levels, models and animations

Based on their own internal Stingray editing features

Pick up your feet, mayflies! Fatshark's co-op rat-whacker Warhammer: Vermintide 2 is getting some new mod tools. It already has a public SDK and modding framework, you say? Ah, but the new mod tools are better. They are a public-facing incarnation of the very same digital spellcraft Fatshark use to create the official levels and characters.

"While the Vermintide 2 Software Development Kit and the Vermintide Modding Framework have been out for years, these mostly only facilitated the development of purely code-related mods," the devs write on the official site. "There was no support for any other type of mod, and so creating mods that involved creating new assets has been either extremely difficult or impossible. But no more!

"The Mod Tools is a public release of our internal Stingray developer tools for Vermintide 2!" they continue. "This powerful set of tools will allow modders to work their magic on both editing and creating anything from custom levels, models, textures, particles, animations, and more! While it will probably take them a little while to cook exciting new mods, this marks a new era for Vermintide 2 modded content!"

OK, that's enough exclamation marks. The new mod tools are available to all owners of the game. You'll be able to find them in your Steam library, listed as "Modding Tools" and "Modding Tools content".

Fatshark have had to make a few "compromises" to get the new mod toolkit finished. "The weapon pack and the level that we mentioned in the past has been put on hold," the devs write. "We still want to get back to that, especially the weapon pack, but for now there is no active development on that. It’s important for us that we have transparency here, and while we are not working on these things, we do stick with our games! We have plans both near and far for Vermintide 2."

The Mod Tools rollout accompanies a change in server support. Hitherto, the Vermintide 2 modding scene has been split between the game's "Official Realm", where only officially sanctioned mods are allowed - "typically reserved for QoL mods that did not affect the experience much", the devs say – and the howling Chaos Wastes of the Modded Realm, which lets you install whatever grievous warpstone chicanery you please, at the cost of having no progression.

The lack of progression in Modded Realm has resulted in these servers "not seeing much use outside of niche communities", Fatshark claim. They're addressing that by, as you may guess, adding a Modded-only offline progression system, allowing players to scoop up loot and XP while performing weird experiments on the simulation.

Fatshark say they no longer have the capacity to keep up with mod approvals in the Official Realm, to say nothing of problems resulting from mods that have stopped receiving updates. They don't seem to have a solution for this, yet. They do, however, have a solution for an on-going lack of players in the dedicated Versus servers: shut down those servers! Let them crumple to dust!

"Versus is still playable, but it will be through community hosted games found through the Custom Game or the Lobby Browser," the devs assure. "This is already how most games of Versus are played, so we don’t think it will be a huge shake up in any shape or form, and it puts more of a focus on the Custom Game format where players have more control over the ruleset."

The shutdown will happen alongside the game's next update – Gifts of the Wolf Father, due in early December, which will rework the game's talent balance, update the weapon icons, and make the glow of different runes easier to distinguish from afar. Look out for more details down the line. In the meantime, please thrill my pointy ears with talk of Vermintide 2 mods. I've never touched that side of the game, and am wondering if there are any Skaven megaprojects I'm missing out on.

#3709. GTA 6 reinvigorates PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series S/X console sales in the US, even at their inflated prices

Despite the far higher prices of PlayStation and Xbox consoles today compared to their launch, or even the same period last year, both brands of console saw a significant boost in US sales leading up to the launch of this generation's biggest game: Grand Theft Auto 6.

In the week ending 14th November, PS5 hardware unit sales registered a 2.4x increase over the same week last year. Xbox wasn't far behind, seeing a 2.3x increase in its own unit sales. That's according to industry analyst Mat Piscatella at Circana, who pulled the data from Circana's retail tracking service, which covers the US retail market.

The PS5 Pro only accounted for less than 10 percent of the PlayStation's total unit sales, by the way, which Piscatella noted was "a LOT better than it has been in recent weeks", and seemingly the result of increased supply.

GTA 6, of course, released on 19th November, so the surge in console hardware sales was clearly driven by the rush to attain consoles before the game came out. And while the GTA 6-driven demand isn't surprising, it's worth noting how much more expensive PS5 and Xbox Series X/S consoles are today.

A standard PS5 today costs $650, compared to $550 a year ago. The PS5 Pro saw a big jump from $750 last November to $900 today. The base Xbox Series X jumped from $650 last year to $800 today, while Series S now costs $500, up from $400.

Even Switch 2, where GTA 6 is not available, saw a notable boost of 40 percent in hardware sales over the same period, driven by The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake and the special edition Zelda Switch 2 console.

Circana's November US video game market report, which releases in December, is already one of the most anticipated this year, for digesting and documenting the GTA 6 effect. Worldwide, GTA 6 sold more than 32.5m copies in one day, making Rockstar's parent company Take-Two $3.79bn (£2.89bn) in revenue. We haven't had any updated official sales figures since; but estimates suggest the sales figure could be well into the 40-millions. Perhaps Rockstar is waiting to hit the nice round 50m sales mark before announcing it.

If you're playing GTA 6, you may want to keep Eurogamer's GTA 6 walkthrough to hand. It has plenty of very helpful guides covering the game's main missions, as well as explainers for mechanics like romance and the criminal profile, and even cheats for when you finish the game.

#3707. Keep the lighthouse on and the villagers obedient in Glagstone, an eerie island city-builder with Macintosh-style graphics

Now coming to Steam, following a Playdate prototype

Glagstone's "1-bit" aesthetic is a homage to Macintosh games of the late 1980s, cut with elements of art deco, Expressionism and film noir, but it looks like that mainly because it began life on lo-fi indie handheld Playdate.

In transplanting this eerie, story-driven city-builder to Steam, developers Valerii Krasnoselskii and Evgenii Kirichenko have fleshed out the tasty throwback art and shored up connections between the game's management and story layers, while leaving the crux of the experience untouched: you are the newly appointed governor of a remote northern island, contested by rival nations. You have come here to harvest the island's rich mineral resources, and now, the island is trying to drive you nuts.

You start by building homes and roads, getting fish to the warehouse, and churning out coal for the Crown. You'll also need to get the local lighthouse operational, so that you can see the city you're maintaining amid recurring fog, storms and darkness.

According to the devs, who've written a longer account of their project for 80.lv, it's supposed to feel like a simple sandbox, at first. But it has a creeping undertow. Visiting ships bring both opportunity and peril – admitting them to port is a gamble. The coastline is worryingly indefinite, in ways that can't quite be attributed to the tides. The locals are secretive, demanding and a little sinister. They talk of strange masked rituals, Silver Ladies, Shed Skins, and coves where you don't go during an eclipse. The Crown's orders, meanwhile, make less and less sense, and the waves keep coughing up peculiar objects. Sometimes, you could swear you hear singing through the surf.

A lot of the associated Dreadful Lore appears to arrive in the form of notebook marginalia, item descriptions, and sailor anecdotes that need to be coaxed forth with the promise of liquor. There are also pop-up events that may shape the morale and loyalty of your townsfolk. Those masked festivals, for example: they'll cost you production, but the glint in the village elder's eye suggests that refusing to give people time off for the Old Listening might be… reckless.

It all feels like an elaborate port fable from Failbetter's Sunless Sea. Or a standalone episode from fellow "1-bit" coastal sojourn World of Horror. You probably don't need me to tell you that Poe and Lovecraft are among the explicit influences. The developers – who are based in Belgrade and Basel - have also taken inspiration from the Svalbard and Novaya Zemlya archipelagoes. I've just googled Svalbard. It has very pretty reindeer. Haven't dug up any reports of kraken and mermaids just yet, but I'm sure they're out there.

Glagstone is coming to PC next year. Catch it on Steam - they're accepting playtest requests. Speaking as a fan of impenetrable marine murk, I think this looks wonderful. The 80.lv piece is worth reading through, however self-promotional - it includes some savoury titbits on how they've modelled the play of radiance between lighthouse beam and roadside lantern. Did you try the Playdate original? Any comments?

#3706. Blizzard adjusts popular World of Warcraft: Forever Battleground to stop players power-grinding rewards

"The overall intent for all of these changes was for games to feel more meaningful."

Many World of Warcraft: Forever players are currently in the midst of a substantial PvP reputation grind. However, this process has been disrupted due to a sudden change to one of the game's battleground PvP arenas.

The battleground in question is Alterac Valley, a 40 person-a-side clash between Alliance and Horde factions, where both sides need to push their forces across a snowy, mountainous map into the opposing faction's base to take down the NPC General waiting there. Alterac Valley is being grinded by max-level players for its gear rewards that are given once reaching "exalted" reputation there. Currently it's some of the best gear available ahead of raids being introduced next month.

Played the intended way, Alterac Valley is a lengthy battle. The Generals on both sides are fearsomely tough but by rushing to capture certain structures on the way to this battle, you can weaken the Generals enough to make them easier to overcome. As such, players have been fast-tracking this PvP instance, skipping smaller objectives and rushing core objectives to get to the Generals as fast as possible. This bypassed a lot of the incidental skirmishing allure of Alterac Valley, but it was an efficient way to quickly gain reputation and Honor points (PvP currency).

But this strategy has been pretty much killed outright as of today. In a post made to the official World of Warcraft forums, community manager Kaivax revealed that the reputation gained from killing the Generals has been drastically reduced, while the reputation gained from killing other NPCs and capturing previously ignored objectives now grants more. Generals are also granted a buff that makes them incredibly strong for the first 20 minutes of a match, which is then reduced for each objective taken.

This is a good change in regard to the experience of playing Alterac Valley. While rushing through was good for players looking to gain reputation quickly, they weren't really playing the Battleground in the way it's meant to be played. The dev post reads: "The overall intent for all of these changes was for games to feel more meaningful while trying to maintain a similar amount of rep gained over a similar playtime within the battleground, even with longer match lengths. There will be fluctuations depending on how successful you are at destroying towers and holding capture points at the end of a match however."

So how has the community reacted? Badly! Taking a gander at community hubs following this change shows plenty of frustration. Take this comment by Reddit user Athrek: "I'm fine with the changes if they give it Rank Points and calendar events. But they've gutted the rep for both sides, extended the time it takes to play, and it still gives zero Rank Points. Now you may as well get to the win condition and then sit there for a few hours, gaining the passive rep cause there's nothing else of value to be had."

It appears as of writing that the reputation gained isn't as much as it was previously, so those playing purely for reputation have been hit. There's another element of frustration which is that those who rushed to level 60 and ground Alterac Valley reputation and rewards before the changes won't be affected by this. Perhaps that's the allure of rushing to level 60!

"This is why the WoW mantra is 'exploit early, exploit often'," writes user Lanienah12. "Some people are already exalted with AV rep and will receive no punishment for it; meanwhile new people will be spending 3x as long." Especially in the wake of the Blackmaw Hold gold exploit being discovered by these frontrunners, there's a growing belief that those taking their time or that are limited by real-life factors are feeling the brunt of these changes.

Microsoft-owned developer platform Github stepped in it earlier today when it posted a message on X celebrating the success of AnyPS5, an open source project that aims to let users port PS5 executables to PC, and then linked that success directly to efforts to port Grand Theft Auto 6 to PC. The message was deleted shortly after it was posted, but not before it was widely noticed and called out for being a very bad idea.

"GTA 6 is finally here, sparking one of the biggest weeks in gaming and open source on Github," the message stated (via Kotaku).

"The repo AnyPS5 has passed 58K stars since its August launch, rewriting PS5 executables to run on Windows and Linux. Does changing where games run cross a legal line? Share your take. Happy GTA VImas!"

Lest there be any misunderstanding, a video that accompanied the post made the GTA 6 connection explicit: "The project rewrites a game's executable so Windows and Linux can run it directly. Performance seems to be the main issue for users wanting to run GTA 6, with one contributor telling the project's community to 'lock in and get your agents to help' if they need to."

And here's the accompanying video from @github's GTA6 tweet https://t.co/crU9cpOWcsNovember 26, 2026

The question of whether or not this sort of thing crosses a legal line has, predictably, sparked debate among those who think they have a clear understanding of the answer. What caught most by surprise, though, is that Github—which is owned by Microsoft—would put forth the question in the first place, implicitly suggesting that it might not. GTA 6 publisher Take-Two Interactive has been pretty aggressive with its efforts to keep recompiled versions of GTA 6 from landing on PC, and I can't imagine it would too thrilled with Github—which, I must emphasize, is owned by Microsoft—telling the world that it might actually be okay to go ahead and vibe-code it up.

That point wasn't missed by redditors, one of whom described it as Github "openly taunting Sony and Rockstar." Even the AnyPS5 subreddit seemed baffled: Redditor superkickstart asked, "Do they have AI running their socials? Lol"

There's also a little bit of irony in the fact that, until earlier this week, the leading effort to get GTA 6 running on PC was based on an Xbox build of the game posted by GTA 6 leaker Cyberleeks. Beyond that, there are also some very obvious questions about how Github (owned by Microsoft) would react to AI-powered ports of, say, other software:

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

The whole thing is weird, really, because it seems like such an obviously bad idea. The only explanation I can come up with is that a social media manager either didn't think about it, didn't understand it (which would be weird in itself for someone doing social media posts for Github), or just had a big ol' brain fart. Whatever the reason, I imagine someone got a good old-fashioned talking-to about it.

I've reached out to Github and Take-Two for comment and will update if I receive a reply.

Andy has been gaming on PCs from the very beginning, starting as a youngster with text adventures and primitive action games on a cassette-based TRS80. From there he graduated to the glory days of Sierra Online adventures and Microprose sims, ran a local BBS, learned how to build PCs, and developed a longstanding love of RPGs, immersive sims, and shooters. He began writing videogame news in 2007 for The Escapist and somehow managed to avoid getting fired until 2014, when he joined the storied ranks of PC Gamer. He covers all aspects of the industry, from new game announcements and patch notes to legal disputes, Twitch beefs, esports, and Henry Cavill. Lots of Henry Cavill.

#3704. Go fishing and fire Hornet out of a cannon in Silksong's December-bound Sea of Sorrow expansion, which Team Cherry say is "unlike anything we’ve done before"

Honest to goodness news for Hollow Knight: Silksong expansion Sea of Sorrow? That I didn’t invent in a dream? Scarcely believable, yet entirely true. The watery DLC is releasing on December 11th 2026, a scant two weeks from now, and as with original Hollow Knight's expansions it’ll be free to those who own the base game. There’s also a new trailer, showing some of the gunpowder-jumping and fishy boss-battling Hornet will get up to while exploring those sorrowful seas.

Hollow Knight: Silksong - Sea of Sorrow - Launch Trailer Watch on YouTube

Keen ramblers through Silksong’s sonorous Pharloom kingdom will note the new, aquatic locales: coral-coated ruins, damp algae forests, and bioluminescent cliffs that crackle with strange blue lighting. A piratical sub-theme also flashes up in a few places, particularly one yarr-ing jellybug boss and Hornet’s newfound talent for launching herself out of cannons as a movement aid.

There also looks to be at least another one of Silksong’s deviously tricky 'Climb a shaft while being chased by rising Bad Liquid' sections, as well as a moment when Hornet tries her claw at silk-fishing. I’m not the most accomplished Silksongist on the planet but I’ve played enough to know that whatever she catches will probably have two phases and a title card.

Or will it? In introducing the release date and trailer, as part of a Cherry Time showcase on the developers’ YouTube channel, Team Cherry claimed Sea of Sorrow is "unlike anything we’ve done before" – so further surprises are likely in store, even if I’d still wager that most of them involve needle violence. More fundamentally, Sea of Sorrow does look considerably larger in scope than any of Hollow Knight’s freebie DLCs, which at most – Godhome, basically – added a small handful of new locations and a smattering of boss challenges. Silksong’s first expansion appears to be showing off multiple new regions, legions of new enemy types, extra traversal mechanics, and that most desired of prizes among soulslike and soulslike-adjacent fans: untold lore.

And it’s out in two weeks? Time to get back in the water.
